//: The complete list of places this OS is allowed to contain assembly, and
why each one cannot be Rust. Enforced by scripts/check-asm-budget.py and
The test for admission is narrow: the construct must be defined by what
the *machine* does to registers around it, before or after the first
instruction of a Rust function could run. An exception vector table is on
this list because the CPU jumps to a fixed offset with the interrupted
context still live in the registers; a scheduler is not, because nothing
about it is architectural once the registers have been saved.
'Convenient in assembly' is not a reason. 'Faster in assembly' is not a
reason either -- measure it, then argue it in the entry.
//max_total_lines: The cap that actually binds. Assembly is a fixed cost here: the list below
is meant to be finished once both architectures boot, and a scheduler, a
filesystem or a driver must add nothing to it. 800 is the full intended
set with headroom, not a target to grow into.
//max_ratio: Backstop only, and deliberately slack. With assembly capped absolutely,
the Rust share is a function of how much OS has been written, so a tight
ratio here would just be measuring how young the tree is. Ratchet it down
as the tree grows; it should never be what fails a build.
//target_ratio: The founding claim: 99.9% Rust. Reached by writing the operating system,
not by shrinking the vector table. At today's ~500 lines of assembly it
needs the tree to pass roughly half a million lines of Rust, so treat it
as the direction of travel that check-asm-budget.py prints every run.

files.reason: The loader's last instructions. Writing CR3 replaces the address space the return address of a Rust function call would live in, so the switch and the jump to the kernel cannot be a call. Also EFER.NXE and CR4.PGE, which are MSR and control-register writes with no Rust spelling and which must happen before the tables that rely on them are installed.

As x86-64, and longer for one architectural reason: TCR_EL1 cannot be reprogrammed under a live translation regime, so the sequence has to turn the MMU off, install MAIR/TCR/TTBR0/TTBR1, and turn it back on. The middle of that runs with the program counter as a physical address. Also `dc civac` cache maintenance, without which the tables written above are invisible once the caches are off.

CPU primitives, one instruction each: `out`/`in` reach the I/O address space, which is not memory and has no Rust syntax; `hlt` and `cli` are CPU state; reading and writing CR3 is a control register. Grows with stage 3 (IDT, TSS, APIC) and must not grow with anything else.

CPU primitives, one instruction each: `dsb`/`isb` are barriers, `tlbi` is TLB maintenance, `wfi` and `msr daifset` are CPU state, and `hvc` is the PSCI call that powers the machine off. Grows with stage 3 (VBAR_EL1, GIC, the generic timer) and must not grow with anything else.

The 256 interrupt entry stubs and the common save/restore path. The CPU enters a handler with the interrupted registers still live and pushes a frame whose shape depends on the vector -- ten of the 256 push an error code and the rest do not -- so no Rust function can be entered and no Rust signature can describe the frame. The stubs are generated by an assembler `.rept`: the same machine code as 256 Rust-emitted blocks, at a twentieth of the lines. Also `int3`, which is how the boot test proves the path works.

The `VBAR_EL1` vector table and its save/restore path. The architecture defines a table of sixteen entries at fixed 128-byte offsets, and that layout *is* the interface -- a Rust array of function pointers is not what the CPU reads. Each entry is far too small for a register save, so it stashes two registers, records which entry it is, and branches to the common path. Also `brk`, for the boot test.
